title: Graph Theory Foundations
summary: Graphs as mathematical structures — connectivity, bipartiteness, Euler/Hamiltonian paths, coloring, and planarity.

slides.markdown:
This Topic is about graphs as **mathematical structures** — what properties they can have and how to reason about them. Traversal, shortest-path, and MST *algorithms* live in graph *algorithms* — this is the structure those algorithms operate on, not a repeat of them.

Think of it as the difference between studying "what shapes can exist" (geometry) versus "how to compute their area" (algorithms) — you need the structural vocabulary before the algorithms make sense.

A graph is vertices (`V`) plus edges (`E`) connecting pairs of them. A vertex's **degree** is its edge count. The **handshake lemma**: the sum of all degrees equals `2|E|`, since every edge contributes exactly 1 to each of its two endpoints' degree counts.

A graph is **dense** if `|E|` is close to the maximum possible (`n(n−1)/2` for undirected), **sparse** if `|E|` is closer to `n`. This distinction drives real engineering choices — dense graphs favor an adjacency *matrix* (`O(1)` edge lookup), sparse graphs favor an adjacency *list* (saves memory).

An undirected graph is **connected** if a path joins every pair of vertices; otherwise it splits into disjoint **components**. Directed graphs: **strongly connected** (directed path both ways) vs **weakly connected** (connected only ignoring direction).

![Strongly vs weakly connected graph](assets/connectivity-diagram.svg)

"Who reaches whom via one-way follows" is strong; citation graphs are typically only weak — papers rarely cite back.

A graph is **bipartite** if its vertices split into two groups such that every edge connects one group to the other — never within the same group. Matching applicants-to-jobs or students-to-dorm-rooms are naturally bipartite.

**The 2-coloring test:** a graph is bipartite iff you can 2-color it with no edge connecting same-colored vertices — equivalently, iff it has **no odd-length cycle**. Run BFS, alternating colors by level; if a vertex needs conflicting colors, it isn't bipartite.

An **Euler path** visits every *edge* exactly once (vertices may repeat); an **Euler circuit** is an Euler path that returns to its start. This is the original graph theory problem — the 1736 **bridges of Königsberg**, where Euler proved no walk could cross each of the 7 bridges exactly once.

**The condition:** a connected graph has an Euler circuit iff every vertex has **even degree**; it has an Euler path (not circuit) iff exactly **0 or 2** vertices have odd degree. Königsberg had 4 land-masses each with odd degree — far more than the 0-or-2 allowed, hence no solution.

A **Hamiltonian path** visits every *vertex* exactly once (edges may be skipped) — deceptively similar wording to Euler paths, but wildly different in difficulty. Checking whether a Hamiltonian path exists is **NP-complete**: no known algorithm solves it faster than roughly trying all vertex orderings in the worst case.

The contrast is the whole point: Euler's condition ("check every vertex's degree") is a simple, fast check; Hamiltonian's condition has no known simple characterization at all — a preview of the P vs NP question covered in [complexity classes](complexity-classes-p-np).

**Graph coloring** assigns colors to vertices so no edge connects same-colored vertices, using as few colors as possible — the minimum is the **chromatic number**. Register allocation in compilers and exam scheduling (no student in two exams at once) both reduce to graph coloring.

The **four color theorem** states any *planar* map can be colored with just 4 colors so no two adjacent regions share a color — famous both for being intuitively surprising and for being one of the first major theorems proved with computer assistance (1976), since a full by-hand case analysis was impractical.

A graph is **planar** if it can be drawn flat with no edges crossing. **Kuratowski's theorem**: planar iff no subdivision of `K₅` (5 vertices, all connected) or `K₃,₃` (two groups of 3, every cross-pair connected).

![K5 and K3,3, the two forbidden planarity subgraphs](assets/planarity-diagram.svg)

`K₃,₃` is the classic "3 houses, 3 utilities, no crossing lines" puzzle — provably impossible.

A **tree** is a connected, acyclic graph — and among the most useful special cases: it has exactly `n−1` edges for `n` vertices (add one more edge to a tree and you create exactly one cycle), and there is a **unique path** between any two vertices.

This uniqueness is what makes trees so predictable to reason about — no ambiguity about "which way" between two nodes, unlike general graphs where multiple paths (and hence multiple costs) can exist between the same pair.

**Wrong belief:** "these two graphs have the same degree sequence (e.g. both have degrees `[3,3,2,2,2,2]`), so they must be the same graph (isomorphic)." **Why it's wrong:** degree sequence only describes *how many* edges touch each vertex, not *which* vertices connect to which — two very differently-shaped graphs can share it by coincidence.

**Correct model:** matching degree sequences is a **necessary but not sufficient** condition for isomorphism — always try to actually construct a vertex-to-vertex mapping that preserves every edge before concluding two graphs are the same structure.
